framework: Our learning framework, based on the linked records. Questions and next connections are our prompts, not a reconstruction of Tim’s private thoughts.

points.label: March 1989 · The proposal
points.title: Put the idea on paper.
points.caption: Archive reproduction of the proposal’s first page.
points.credit: Image: CERN · Educational and informational use. Displayed from CERN’s archive; copyright retained.
points.fact: He proposed connecting information through distributed hypertext to address the loss of knowledge at CERN.
points.question: What problem did those circles and links describe?

decision.question: How could people find knowledge as a project changed?
decision.change: The document explains his intended approach. Working software is the next milestone to investigate.
decision.next: What would a working demonstration need?

points.label: 1990 · First Web server
points.title: Give the idea a working machine.
points.caption: The original NeXT workstation, photographed on display in 2005. The photograph is later than the invention.
points.credit: Photo: Coolcaesar · CC BY-SA 3.0. Original 2008 upload; resized and compressed.
points.fact: His first Web server and browser ran on a NeXT computer at CERN.
points.question: What did one computer need to send a page to another?

decision.question: Could linked documents work through running software?
decision.change: A server and browser were working by the end of 1990.
decision.next: How could somebody on another kind of computer participate?

points.label: 1990 · Browser and editor
points.title: Let people follow links and edit.
points.caption: An archived screenshot of a later WorldWideWeb version. It does not show the first run in 1990.
points.credit: Screenshot: Ck_mpk; PNG adaptation: FedericoMP, 2008 · CC BY-SA 3.0. Image unchanged.
points.fact: WorldWideWeb combined reading linked documents with editing them.
points.question: How is a place for making knowledge different from a place for only reading?

decision.question: Could somebody both read and create linked documents?
decision.change: The original browser supported editing, but required a NeXT computer.
decision.next: What simpler browser could reach more people?

points.label: 1990–1991 · The first website
points.title: Explain how others could take part.
points.caption: A 2021 screenshot of an early Web page in CERN’s browser emulator. This is a later reconstruction, not a 1991 screenshot.
points.credit: CERN / Tim Berners-Lee; uploaded by Erick Soares3, 2021 · Public-domain record. Image unchanged.
points.fact: The first website explained the Web project, hypertext and ways to use the system.
points.question: What would a newcomer need to know before trying it?

decision.question: How could a newcomer learn what the project offered?
decision.change: The website explained the project and linked to further information.
decision.next: How could others try it and contribute?

points.label: 1991 · Show people the Web
points.title: Let other people try the idea.
points.caption: Berners-Lee demonstrating the Web at Hypertext 1991, San Antonio.
points.credit: Image: CERN · Educational and informational use. Displayed from CERN’s archive; copyright retained.
points.fact: A working demonstration gave people a chance to see and question the system.
points.question: What might another person notice that its creator had missed?

decision.question: What could people discover by trying the working software?
decision.change: The photograph shows the demonstration. The archive caption gives no detailed account of the audience’s feedback.
decision.next: What feedback would be useful to investigate?

points.label: 30 April 1993 · Open the software
points.title: Allow others to build on it.
points.caption: CERN’s document releasing key Web software into the public domain.
points.credit: Image: CERN · Educational and informational use. Displayed from CERN’s archive; copyright retained.
points.fact: The release covered the basic line-mode client, server and common-code library. Web software had circulated earlier.
points.question: What becomes possible when others can use and change the software?

decision.question: What permission did other developers need?
decision.change: CERN permitted use, copying, modification and distribution of the released components.
decision.next: How could different implementations remain compatible?

points.label: October 1994 · W3C
points.title: Help different systems work together.
points.caption: A CERN portrait dated 1994. It is not a photograph of W3C’s founding meeting.
points.credit: Image: CERN · Educational and informational use. Displayed from CERN’s archive; copyright retained.
points.fact: He founded W3C at MIT in cooperation with CERN to coordinate Web standards.
points.question: Which rules must people share so their different tools can connect?

decision.question: How could independently developed tools share a common Web?
decision.change: W3C provided a community for coordinating Web standards.
decision.next: Which decisions would need continuing public discussion?

points.label: 26 June 1998 · The next questions
points.title: Keep questioning what comes next.
points.caption: Speaking at CERN’s “Internet, Web, What’s next?” conference.
points.credit: Image: CERN · Educational and informational use. Displayed from CERN’s archive; copyright retained.
points.fact: The invention was already established, while discussion about its future continued.
points.question: What new problems can appear after an invention succeeds?

decision.question: What questions remain after a technology becomes established?
decision.change: The photograph preserves his appearance at a conference about what would come next.
decision.next: What new evidence would change a prediction about the Web?

points.label: 2003 · A wider conversation
points.title: Take the conversation beyond software.
points.caption: Berners-Lee with Kofi Annan during the World Summit on the Information Society.
points.credit: Image: CERN · Educational and informational use. Displayed from CERN’s archive; copyright retained.
points.fact: The historical record includes international discussion as well as code and computers.
points.question: Who should have a voice in a technology used across countries?

decision.question: Who should participate in discussions about information technology?
decision.change: The photograph places him in an international conversation about the information society.
decision.next: Whose perspectives should a future discussion include?

points.label: 13 March 2009 · Remember the collaborators
points.title: Look back with other contributors.
points.caption: Ben Segal, Tim Berners-Lee and Robert Cailliau beside the NeXT at the proposal’s twentieth anniversary.
points.credit: Photo: Maximilien Brice, CERN · CC BY 4.0. Resized and compressed.
points.fact: This reunion is a later reflection on the early work, not a photograph from 1989.
points.question: Whose contributions can disappear when a story focuses on only one inventor?

decision.question: How can a history acknowledge several contributors?
decision.change: The 2009 reunion brings three contributors together beside the original machine.
decision.next: Which other people and earlier inventions should we follow?

points.label: 24 September 2014 · Public recognition
points.title: Recognise the person in the photograph.
points.caption: Berners-Lee arriving at the Guildhall to receive the Honorary Freedom of the City of London.
points.credit: Photo: Paul Clarke · CC BY-SA 4.0. Resized and compressed.
points.fact: This is the photograph from your app. Paul Clarke is its photographer.
points.question: What do a photograph’s date and credit tell us—and what do they leave unknown?

decision.question: What can a photograph tell us about a person’s work?
decision.change: Its date, occasion and photographer establish the photograph’s context.
decision.next: Which account or document would answer the next question?

points.label: 2025–2026 · Tell his own story
points.title: Return to his own account.
points.caption: The UK paperback cover of This Is for Everyone, shown on his official book website. The memoir first appeared in 2025.
points.credit: Cover: official book website / publisher; copyright retained. Reduced for this educational discussion.
points.fact: His own memoir offers a further route into the experiences and decisions behind the Web.
points.question: Which recollection could you compare with a document written at the time?

decision.question: How can a later recollection add to an earlier record?
decision.change: The memoir is a later personal account, distinct from documents written during the invention.
decision.next: Where do recollections and contemporary records agree or differ?
